Studies conducted between 2004 and 2013 across seven African countries have compared the outcomes of HIV care among adults and older adults, as reported in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) in 2014. 2. Research by Lamb et al. (2014) highlights the high rates of attrition both before and after the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) among youth aged 15–24 enrolled in HIV care programs. 3. Grimsrud et al. (2014) analyzed the outcomes of ART over a decade of program expansion in African and Asian HIV programs, emphasizing the importance of long-term cohort studies. 4. Koech et al. (2014) examined the characteristics and outcomes of HIV-infected youth and young adolescents in Kenya, providing insights into the challenges faced by this demographic in accessing and adhering to care. 5. Vinikoor et al. (2014) demonstrated that the age at which ART is initiated significantly predicts immune recovery, mortality, and loss to follow-up among HIV-infected adults in urban Zambia. 6. Berheto et al. (2014) identified predictors of loss to follow-up among patients living with HIV/AIDS after initiating ART, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions to improve retention. 7. Bygrave et al. (2012) reported on ART outcomes among adolescents and youth in rural Zimbabwe, highlighting the unique challenges faced by this population in accessing and adhering to treatment. 8. Ngokosin et al. (2015) explored the treatment and care needs of adolescents living with HIV, emphasizing the importance of timely and consistent medication adherence. 9. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed global standards for adolescent-friendly health services, aiming to improve the quality and accessibility of care for young people. 10. Studies such as those by Mavhu et al. (2013) and Denison et al. (2015) have focused on enhancing psychosocial support and self-management strategies for adolescents living with HIV, demonstrating the critical role of caregiver involvement. 11. Research has also explored the effectiveness of mobile health interventions, such as text messaging systems, to support adherence to ART among youth, as seen in studies by Belzer et al. (2014) and Franklin et al. (2006). 12. The WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care emphasize the importance of monitoring and evaluation (M&E) frameworks to assess program effectiveness and address gaps in service delivery. 13. The guidelines propose a set of 50 national indicators, including 10 global indicators, to monitor the HIV care cascade, from prevention to treatment and care, ensuring alignment with international standards. 14. Data collection and disaggregation by age, sex, and key populations are critical for tailoring interventions and maximizing the impact of HIV programs, while maintaining confidentiality and security of patient information. 15. The WHO underscores the need for robust M&E systems to track patient retention, ART adherence, and viral suppression, as well as to evaluate the impact of differentiated models of care. 16. Facility-based reporting systems, population-based surveys, and facility assessments are key sources of strategic information for monitoring the HIV response at both national and global levels. 17. The integration of HIV services with other health programs, such as tuberculosis (TB) and maternal health, is essential for improving outcomes and addressing comorbidities. 18. The WHO's guidelines also highlight the importance of involving civil society in M&E activities to better understand the experiences and needs of people living with HIV and key populations. 19. This summary reflects the detailed content of the references and guidelines provided, focusing on the key findings and recommendations for improving HIV care and treatment outcomes.
